questions.question: The theoretical lattice energy of CaCl2 is -2223 kJ mol-1. Explain why the experimental (Born-Haber) lattice energy is more exothermic than this theoretical value.
questions.answer: The theoretical value assumes purely ionic bonding; the real compound has covalent character from polarisation of Cl- by Ca2+, giving a more exothermic experimental value
steps: The theoretical lattice energy is calculated from electrostatics, assuming perfectly spherical ions and purely ionic bonding.
Calcium ions have a high charge density (2+ and small), so they polarise the large chloride ions.
This polarisation gives the bonding some covalent character, which the ionic model does not include.
The extra covalent bonding makes the lattice more stable, so the experimental lattice energy is more exothermic than -2223 kJ mol-1.

questions.question: Explain the trend in theoretical lattice energies of the Group 2 chlorides on descending Group 2.
questions.answer: Lattice energy becomes less exothermic down the group because the cations get larger, so charge density falls and the electrostatic attraction weakens
steps: Going down Group 2, the metal ions get larger because they have more electron shells.
The 2+ charge stays the same, so the charge density (charge/radius) decreases.
Weaker attraction between the larger cation and the chloride ions means less energy is released when the lattice forms.
So the lattice energy becomes less exothermic on descending the group.

questions.question: Which compound would be expected to have the least exothermic lattice energy? Options: A calcium chloride, B magnesium chloride, C potassium bromide, D sodium bromide.
questions.answer: C - potassium bromide
steps: Lattice energy depends on the charges of the ions (product of charges) and on the ionic radii.
CaCl2 and MgCl2 have 2+ cations, so their lattice energies are very exothermic.
KBr and NaBr have 1+ and 1- ions, so they are much less exothermic.
K+ is larger than Na+, so its charge density is lower and the lattice energy is less exothermic.
So potassium bromide has the least exothermic lattice energy, option C.

questions.question: Which compound would be expected to have the largest difference between experimental (Born-Haber) and theoretical lattice energies? Options: A calcium chloride, B magnesium chloride, C potassium bromide, D sodium bromide.
questions.answer: B - magnesium chloride
steps: The difference between experimental and theoretical values is largest when the bonding has the most covalent character.
Covalent character increases with the polarising power of the cation (high charge and small size).
Mg2+ is the smallest and most highly charged cation of the four, so it has the greatest polarising power.
So MgCl2 has the most covalent character and the largest difference, option B.

questions.question: The standard enthalpy change of solution of KCl is +17 kJ mol-1 and its solubility is 359 g dm-3 at 298 K. Which explains the solubility? Options: A hydration enthalpy of K+ and lattice energy of KCl are exothermic, B (garbled option about enthalpy values), C total entropy change on dissolving is positive, D total entropy change on dissolving is negative.
questions.answer: C - the total entropy change when KCl dissolves is positive
steps: The enthalpy change of solution is endothermic (+17 kJ mol-1), so enthalpy alone does not favour dissolving.
Dissolving disperses the ions into solution, which increases the entropy of the system.
The entropy of the surroundings also changes as the solution cools, so the total entropy change can be positive.
A positive total entropy change makes dissolving feasible, so option C is the explanation.

questions.topic: True Statement About Hydration And Solution
questions.question: Which statement is true? A The enthalpy change of hydration of an ion is always negative; B the enthalpy change of solution of an ionic compound is always negative; C an endothermic enthalpy change of solution means the compound is insoluble; D the more exothermic the lattice energy, the more soluble the compound.
questions.answer: A - the enthalpy change of hydration of an ion is always negative
steps: Hydration is the process of an ion becoming surrounded by water molecules, which releases energy as ion-dipole bonds form.
So the enthalpy change of hydration is always exothermic, i.e. negative (option A is true).
The enthalpy change of solution can be positive (endothermic), as for KCl, so B is false.
An endothermic solution does not mean insoluble, so C is false; a more exothermic lattice energy makes solubility less likely, so D is false.

questions.question: The reduction of iron(III) oxide by carbon monoxide has deltaH = -24.8 kJ mol-1 and deltaS = +15.2 J mol-1 K-1. Explain why the reaction should be feasible at any temperature.
questions.answer: deltaH is negative and deltaS is positive, so deltaG = deltaH - T deltaS is negative at all temperatures
steps: Feasibility requires deltaG = deltaH - T deltaS to be negative.
deltaH = -24.8 kJ mol-1 is negative, so the first term always makes deltaG negative.
deltaS = +15.2 J mol-1 K-1 is positive, so -T deltaS is also negative for any temperature above 0 K.
Both terms are negative, so deltaG is negative at all temperatures and the reaction is feasible at any temperature.

questions.topic: Effect Of Temperature On Total Entropy
questions.question: Explain how an increase in temperature would affect the total entropy change of the reduction of iron(III) oxide by carbon monoxide. No calculation is required.
questions.answer: The total entropy change decreases with rising temperature, because the surroundings term (-deltaH/T) gets smaller while the system term stays constant
steps: deltaStotal = deltaSsystem + deltaSsurroundings.
deltaSsystem = +15.2 J K-1 mol-1 is constant with temperature.
deltaSsurroundings = -deltaH / T = +24 800 / T, which is positive but gets smaller as T increases.
So deltaStotal falls as T increases, although it stays positive and the reaction remains feasible.

questions.topic: Agreement Of Theoretical And Experimental Values
questions.question: The table gives lattice energies of barium oxide and magnesium iodide and the percentage difference between theoretical and experimental values. Explain why there is closer agreement for barium oxide than for magnesium iodide.
questions.answer: BaO is more ionic: the oxide ion is small and highly charged but not very polarisable, while MgI2 has a small cation and a large polarisable iodide ion, giving more covalent character
steps: Theoretical lattice energies assume purely ionic bonding with spherical ions.
Barium oxide is made of a large, low-charge-density Ba2+ ion and the small O2- ion, so the bonding is close to purely ionic.
Magnesium iodide has a small, highly polarising Mg2+ ion and a large, easily polarised I- ion.
Polarisation adds covalent character to MgI2, so the real lattice energy differs much more from the ionic theoretical value.
Hence agreement is closer for barium oxide than for magnesium iodide.

questions.topic: Theoretical Versus Experimental Lattice Energy For MgCl2
questions.question: Explain the difference between the theoretical lattice energy of MgCl2 (-2326 kJ mol-1) and the experimental (Born-Haber) value.
questions.answer: The real MgCl2 has covalent character from polarisation of Cl- by the small, highly charged Mg2+, which the ionic theoretical value ignores
steps: The theoretical value assumes perfect ionic bonding with point charges.

questions.question: Explain why, when magnesium reacts with chlorine, MgCl2 is formed rather than MgCl3.
questions.answer: Magnesium loses two electrons to form Mg2+ with a noble gas configuration; removing a third electron needs a very large amount of energy that is not recovered in lattice formation
steps: Magnesium has two outer electrons; removing these gives Mg2+ with a stable noble gas (neon) arrangement.

The energy released by forming the extra lattice bonds is not large enough to pay for this third ionisation.
So the most stable product is MgCl2, not MgCl3.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the term enthalpy change of hydration.
questions.answer: The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions dissolves in water to form an infinitely dilute solution (hydrated ions)
steps: It is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of gaseous ions is hydrated (surrounded by water molecules).
The process is done under standard conditions and forms an infinitely dilute solution.
It is always exothermic because bonds form between the ions and water molecules.

questions.topic: Expression For Enthalpy Change Of Solution
questions.question: Complete the expression for the enthalpy change of solution of CuCl2 using the enthalpy changes of hydration and the lattice energy: deltaH(sol) = ?
questions.answer: deltaH(sol) = -LE + deltaH(hyd, Cu2+) + 2 deltaH(hyd, Cl-)
steps: Dissolving breaks the lattice: this takes in energy equal to -LE, since LE is negative.
Hydrating the ions releases energy: deltaH(hyd) for Cu2+ and for each Cl- (two Cl- ions).
So deltaH(sol) = -LE + deltaH(hyd, Cu2+) + 2 x deltaH(hyd, Cl-).

questions.question: The enthalpy change of hydration of Cu+ is -593 kJ mol-1. Explain why the hydration enthalpy of Cu+ is much less exothermic than that of Cu2+.
questions.answer: Cu+ has a lower charge (1+) than Cu2+ (2+), so it has a lower charge density and attracts water molecules less strongly
steps: Hydration enthalpy depends on the charge density of the ion (charge divided by radius).
Cu2+ has twice the charge of Cu+ for a similar size, so it has a much higher charge density.
Cu2+ therefore attracts water molecules more strongly and releases more energy on hydration.
Cu+ has a lower charge density, so its hydration enthalpy is much less exothermic.
